messages.subject: Variable scaling and prior selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to build an observed path model using blavaan (including mediation).
As I understand it correctly (from e.g., Kline, 2016), the variances of the observed variables should be roughly equal for stable estimation (convergence). As I prepare my observed variables, I multiplied some variables with 100 or .001, to make the variance to be around 10-100 factors of magnitude.

For an imaginary situation using my dataset, let's say I had:

Var(X1) =  555463.1
Var(X2) = 0.01078679
Var(X3) = 577.8891 , and
Var(X4) = 1.676907

I multiplied .001 for X1, 10 for X2, and .06 for X3 (because X3 was based on measures per minute). Then the new variance became roughly comparable:
Var(X1) =  0.5554631
Var(X2) = 1.078679
Var(X3) = 2.080401 , and
Var(X4) = 1.676907

Using the transformed dataset, I initially ran lavaan, and the model converged with excellent fit (CFI = 1; SRMR = .05, RMSEA = .000 95%CI = .000 - .13).

Then, I wanted to fit the same model (used the same model syntax) using blavaan, but the model did not fit well (BCFI = .295; BRMSEA = .780). I wonder why this might be, but I came to the conclusion that this may be due to my prior specification. For each of the regression parameters, I used normal(0, 1), and maybe this is the issue (because the variable scales are different even after the transformation).

What might cause this kind of issue in blavaan? If the issue is that of prior, I wonder if anyone could point me in the right direction of how to specify priors for each regression parameter, given the magnitude of the variances is different. Also, I am assuming that using z-scores for observed variables should be avoided because it makes the matrix into a correlation matrix, and covariance information is lost (see this post at lavaan community <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Jq8oEuURbE0/m/bLN18npHCQAJ> ).

 Thanks for reading the question, and looking forward to hearing your views.

Best,
Masaki

messages.subject: Re: Variable scaling and prior selection
messages.body_plain:
Masaki

It would be helpful if you sahre the full syntax.

A couple if ideas, you could use the DIC pD for the blavfitindices, we have seen that in some cases with large differences ebtween the frequentist and bayesian, migt be for differences in the pD calculations

blavFitIndices(fit, pD="dic")

When the metric of the variables are not relevant by temselves (I imagine this is the case as you are already transforming the data ) it is not uncommon to do z-core transformations, you would see that in a lot of bayesian tutorials. The advantage of this is that it makes it easier to think about priors. If you ave z-score variables a prior N(0, 1) is very reasonable.

Also, the issue of priors might on the center of the distriution, and not the SD, as you already ran the model with lavaan, you can check if the estmates are very far from 0, this might be what needs to be adjusted, more than the SD

messages.subject: Re: Variable scaling and prior selection
messages.body_plain:
Thank you so much for the reply.

As you might have expected, I found an error in syntax (did not specify means) but Lavaan fit okay even without it (although correction increased the fit). Blavaan model significantly improved after allowing the mean structure (maybe it was due to model misspecification).

As for the z-score, I still wonder why z-scoring is okay (as I see many people discourage for the reason of retaining the covariance structure). Is this something unique to Bayesian SEM?
Now that you brought this to my attention, I found in Asparouhov et al. (2015) the following line:

"1. Choose a uniform metric for the variables, for example, by standardizing the variables when the model is scale free (no parameter equalities across variables), so that scale issues do not interfere with prior settings (see Muthén & Asparouhov, 2012). "　(Asparouhov et al., 2015).

Is this the reason why we could z-score under BSEM? I would appreciate any information about this.

Thank you so much!

Best,
Masaki

messages.subject: Re: Variable scaling and prior selection
messages.body_plain:
Masaki

This is similar to the fact that variance is the unbias measure of variability, while the standar deviation is bias. But we still use the SD for a lot of things instead of the variance

So, when we use standardized metrics, we might lose some information, but in egenral that lost is very small

And yes, the standardized is interesting for priors because it becomes a lot easier to define them, in function of the standardized parameters, while commonly for their natural metric you might need to consider further the priors related to their metrics.

When I wouldnt recommend this would be in scnearios where measurement invariance is relevant, in this type of cases the metric and its differences are of interest itself

Thank you very much for the follow-up. I now see the reason that the use of z-score may not be a huge issue unless measurement invariance (strong invariance…?) is the purpose of the analysis.

Best,
Masaki
